steps.text: Write the history section of an encyclopedia article on the arithmetic logic unit (ALU), covering where the idea came from, early computer and integrated-circuit ALUs, microprocessors, and modern ALUs.

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The ALU concept was proposed by the mathematician John von Neumann in 1945, in a report on the foundations for a new computer called the EDVAC.

In the infancy of the Information Age, electronic circuitry had relatively high cost, size and power consumption. Because of this, all the early computers had a serial ALU which operated on one data bit at a time, although they often presented a wider word size to programmers. The 1951 Whirlwind I was the first computer to have multiple parallel discrete single-bit ALU circuits. It used sixteen of these "math units" so that it could operate on 16-bit words.

Fairchild introduced the first ALU-like device implemented as an integrated circuit in 1967. This was the Fairchild 3800, and it consisted of an eight-bit arithmetic unit with accumulator. It only supported adds and subtracts, and no logic functions.

Soon full integrated-circuit ALUs emerged, for example four-bit ALUs like the Am2901 and 74181. These devices were typically "bit slice" capable. This means they had "carry look ahead" signals which made it easier to use multiple interconnected ALU chips to create an ALU with a wider word size. These devices became popular quickly and were used widely in bit-slice minicomputers.

In the early 1970s microprocessors began to appear. Transistors had become smaller, but even so there was sometimes not enough die space for a full-word-width ALU, so some early microprocessors used a narrow ALU that needed multiple cycles per machine language instruction. One example of this is the popular Zilog Z80, which did eight-bit additions with a four-bit ALU. Over time transistor geometries shrank more, following Moore's law, and it became feasible to build wider ALUs on microprocessors.

Transistors on modern integrated circuits (ICs) are orders of magnitude smaller than the ones on the early microprocessors, and this makes it possible to fit highly complex ALUs on ICs. Many modern ALUs today have wide word widths, and architectural enhancements like barrel shifters and binary multipliers, which let them do operations in a single clock cycle that would have needed multiple operations on earlier ALUs.

ALUs can be realized as mechanical, electro-mechanical or electronic circuits, and in recent years there has been research into biological ALUs (for example actin-based ones).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Mathematician John von Neumann proposed the ALU concept in 1945, in a report on the foundations for a new computer called the EDVAC.[1]

The cost, size and power consumption of electronic circuitry were relatively high throughout the infancy of the Information Age. As a result, all early computers had a serial ALU that operated on one data bit at a time, although they often presented a wider word size to programmers. The first computer with multiple parallel discrete single-bit ALU circuits was the 1951 Whirlwind I, which used sixteen such "math units" to operate on 16-bit words.

In 1967, Fairchild introduced the first ALU-like device implemented as an integrated circuit, the Fairchild 3800, which consisted of an eight-bit arithmetic unit with accumulator. It supported only adds and subtracts, with no logic functions.[2]

Full integrated-circuit ALUs soon emerged, including four-bit ALUs such as the Am2901 and 74181. These devices were typically "bit slice" capable, meaning they had "carry look ahead" signals that made it easier to use multiple interconnected ALU chips to create an ALU with a wider word size. They quickly became popular and were widely used in bit-slice minicomputers.

Microprocessors began appearing in the early 1970s. Even though transistors had become smaller, there was sometimes not enough die space for a full-word-width ALU, so some early microprocessors used a narrow ALU that needed multiple cycles per machine language instruction. One example is the popular Zilog Z80, which performed eight-bit additions with a four-bit ALU.[3] Over time, transistor geometries shrank further, following Moore's law, and it became feasible to build wider ALUs on microprocessors.

Modern integrated circuit (IC) transistors are orders of magnitude smaller than those of the early microprocessors, which makes it possible to fit highly complex ALUs on ICs. Today many modern ALUs have wide word widths and architectural enhancements such as barrel shifters and binary multipliers that let them perform, in a single clock cycle, operations that would have needed multiple operations on earlier ALUs.

ALUs can be realized as mechanical, electro-mechanical or electronic circuits[4] and, in recent years, research into biological ALUs has been carried out[5,6] (for example, actin-based).[7]
